content: Brugia timori is a parasitic nematode, specifically a filarial roundworm, that causes a disease known as Timor filariasis. This disease was first described in 1965, but the identification of Brugia timori as the causative organism was not established until 1977. In the same year, the mosquito species Anopheles barbirostris was identified as the primary vector responsible for transmitting this parasite. The microfilariae of Brugia timori are morphologically distinct from those of Brugia malayi and Wuchereria bancrofti. They are longer and have a cephalic space with a length-to-width ratio of approximately 3:1. Additionally, the sheath of Brugia timori does not stain pink with Giemsa stain, unlike the sheaths of Brugia malayi and Wuchereria bancrofti. Brugia timori filariasis, like other human filarial infections, manifests with acute febrile episodes and chronic lymphedema. The life cycle of Brugia timori is similar to that of Wuchereria bancrofti and Brugia malayi, resulting in nocturnal periodicity of symptoms. This parasite has so far been found exclusively in the Lesser Sunda Islands of Indonesia. Its distribution is geographically restricted to areas inhabited by its mosquito vector, which breeds in rice fields. A study conducted in Mainang village on Alor Island reported microfilariae in the blood of 157 out of 586 individuals (27%), with 77 of them (13%) exhibiting lymphedema of the leg. Treatment for Brugia timori filariasis has shown promise with the use of anthelmintic drugs such as diethylcarbamazine and albendazole. Some researchers are optimistic that this disease could potentially be eradicated.
